item.title: Tele-Resuscitation in Prehospital Care: Expanding Remote Guidance
Emergency Department-Administered Extended-Release Buprenorphine After Fentanyl Overdose Reversed by Emergency Medical Services With Naloxone
item.description:
Background: Emergency Medical Services (EMS) providers are on the frontline of the opioid epidemic and administered naloxone to reverse suspected overdose over 442,000 times in 2024. Interest in EMS-initiated sublingual (SL) buprenorphine (BUP) exists; however, initiation of month-long extended-release buprenorphine (XR-BUP) in the immediate postoverdose period has not yet been described. The high risk of death from repeat overdose in patients with opioid use disorder (OUD) could be reduced by administration of XR-BUP. The purpose of this case report is to highlight the utility of EMS-initiated SL-BUP followed by XR-BUP to potentially improve care linkage and adherence to medication-assisted OUD treatment.

Case report: A bystander call to 911 dispatched a Basic Life Support (BLS) unit to an unresponsive 30-year-old man found with fentanyl-smoking paraphernalia. First responders administered 8 mg of intranasal naloxone. Paramedics arrived 8 min later and assessed the patient to be in opioid withdrawal with a Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) score of 22. The patient reported using heroin or fentanyl and methamphetamine daily. After consent, paramedics administered 16 mg of SL-BUP. In the ED, an addiction medicine consult service administered a 300-mg monthly XR-BUP formulation. WHY SHOULD AN EMERGENCY PHYSICIAN BE AWARE OF THIS?: We report that rapid transition from naloxone reversal of overdose and EMS initiated SL-BUP to month-long XR-BUP is possible during a single emergency medicine encounter using a stepwise clinical pathway. We hope our observations encourage further prospective study of the intervention described as this may link patients to medication assisted OUD treatment, which decreases mortality in patients with OUD.

Bascombe K, Patregnani M, Gubac D, Authelet K, Hern G, Anderson E

item.title: Massive Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding in an Adolescent Patient: A Case Report
item.description:
Background: Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding in pediatric patients arises from diverse etiologies that vary across age groups. Although it is an uncommon cause of life-threatening hemorrhagic shock, prompt recognition and management are essential. Owing to the infrequency of hemorrhagic shock from GI bleeding in pediatrics, emergency physicians may lack familiarity with its diagnosis and management. Furthermore, multiple etiologies may coexist and may not be detected during the initial esophagogastroduodenoscopy, increasing the risk of premature diagnostic closure.

Case report: A 17-year-old boy with a history of plaque psoriasis was transported by ambulance to the pediatric emergency department of an urban level one trauma center, presenting with copious hematemesis and hemodynamic instability. Initial resuscitation in the emergency department included blood transfusion, followed by admission to the pediatric intensive care unit. The first endoscopic evaluation by pediatric gastroenterology identified duodenal erosion; however, the patient experienced further large-volume bleeding out of proportion to these findings. A subsequent endoscopy revealed a Dieulafoy lesion, which was treated successfully. The patient was ultimately discharged home and has remained stable during long-term follow-up. WHY SHOULD AN EMERGENCY PHYSICIAN BE AWARE OF THIS?: Although severe GI bleeding in pediatric patients is uncommon, emergency physicians must quickly identify hemorrhagic shock across all age groups and be familiar with the broad differential diagnoses that vary by age. Initial management must prioritize airway protection and hemodynamic stabilization as a bridge to definitive intervention. Clinicians should recognize the limitations of endoscopic gastroduodenoscopy and consider the potential for concurrent sources of bleeding that may necessitate additional intervention. © 2025 Elsevier Inc. item.title: Birthday Blues: Clinical Patterns of Emergency Department Visits Surrounding Birthdays
item.description:
Background: Smaller studies have suggested that patients are more likely to present to the emergency department around the time of their birthdays. However, no multi-year analysis has been performed within the U.S. to uncover a possible association between birthdays and presentation to the emergency department (ED).

Objective: The objective of this study was to evaluate the overall frequency year after year of visits to the Emergency Department and the medical conditions most frequently encountered around the time of a birthday.

Methods: We studied emergency department visits from May 2018 to May 2024 at a Level 1 Trauma Center in a metropolitan city in the U.S.. Our analysis assessed the interval before or after ED presentation with respect to a patient's birthday. We utilized timeframes of ± 7 days (7 d) of one's birthday, ± 14 days (14 d), and ± 30 days (30 d) for analysis. We then conducted a descriptive analysis comparing proportions, standardized ratios (SR), and obtaining predictive probabilities from a multivariate logistic regression model.

Results: Of the 310,047 unique ED visits from 2018 to 2024, 12,650 visits were within ±7d of a patient's birthday. There were a greater than expected number of presentations ±7 d for all genders and age groups (particularly those <18 years old), and for those identifying as Asians. When looking at the role of chief complaint, individuals with a chief complaint related to Psychiatric/Toxicology, Trauma, Dermatologic, and Musculoskeletal concerns had a higher incidence of ED presentation ±7 d.

Conclusion: Across all populations, birthdays appear to be associated with an elevated risk of serious illness.

Akinosho K, Grossestreuer AV, Grossman SA
